abstract: Human-pathogenic coronaviruses differ dramatically in pathogenicity but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that highly pathogenic coronaviruses trigger necroptosis in the infected cells and lung tissues, whereas necroptosis is not detected in cells infected by seasonal coronavirus. Mechanistically, highly pathogenic coronaviruses produce Z-RNA, activate ZBP1 and initiates necroptotic cell death signaling, triggering necroinflammation and lung injury. In contrast, seasonal coronaviruses produce little to no Z-RNA, and do not activate necroptosis. Importantly, small-molecule inhibition of necroptosis attenuates inflammatory cytokine expression and markedly ameliorates lung damage in mice infected with all three highly pathogenic coronaviruses, independent of virus clearance. Overall, our study identifies necroptosis as a dominant mediator of coronavirus pathogenesis, and positions necroptosis blockade as a new therapeutic target against severe coronavirus diseases.
hook: Deadly coronaviruses trigger a cell death pathway seasonal ones skip, and blocking it spares mouse lungs.
hook_turn: and blocking it spares mouse lungs.
summary: Highly pathogenic coronaviruses make Z-RNA, which activates the sensor ZBP1 and sets off necroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death. Seasonal coronaviruses barely do this. A small-molecule blocker reduced lung damage in infected mice without clearing the virus. Evidence is from cells and mice, so benefit in people is untested.
title: Necroptosis is a targetable driver of severe coronavirus pathogenesis
